rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī estimates the Qurʾānic sciences at fifty categories and a further vast total calculated by multiplying the Qurʾān’s words by four.
rows.anchor: ذكر القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي في كتاب قانون التأويل إن علوم القرآن خمسون علما

rows.speaker: بعض السلف
rows.claim: Some early authorities say each Qurʾānic word has an outward sense, an inward sense, a limit, and a point of departure; relations among words exceed human enumeration.
rows.anchor: قال بعض السلف إذ لكل كلمة ظاهر وباطن وحد ومقطع

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī groups the Qurʾān’s core subjects into monotheism, reminder—including promise, warning, Paradise, Hell, and purification—and rulings, including duties and commands.
rows.anchor: قال وأم علوم القرآن ثلاثة أقسام توحيد وتذكير وأحكام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fātiḥa is the Mother of the Book because it contains all three fields: monotheism through 1:4, rulings in 1:5, and reminder from 1:6 onward.
rows.anchor: ولهذا المعنى صارت فاتحة الكتاب أم الكتاب لأن فيها الأقسام الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ equals a third of the Qurʾān is explained either as a reward granted by God or as a meaning-based division, since it contains monotheism.
rows.anchor: وقيل ثلثه فى المعنى لأن القرآن ثلاثة أقسام كما ذكرنا وهذه السورة اشتملت على التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for the title “Mother of the Book” is that al-Fātiḥa precedes the rest of the Qurʾān as a mother precedes a daughter.
rows.anchor: وقيل صارت أما لأنها مقدمة على القرآن بالقبلية والأم قبل البنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation of “Opening” is that al-Fātiḥa opens the gates of Paradise, as discussed elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وقيل سميت فاتحة لأنها تفتح أبواب الجنة على وجوه مذكورة فى مواضعها

rows.speaker: أبو الحكم بن برجان
rows.claim: Ibn Barrajān divides Qurʾānic knowledge into God’s names and attributes, prophethood and its proofs, and legal obligation and trial; the last is hardest because it is unfamiliar and neglected.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحكم بن برجان في كتاب الإرشاد وجملة القرآن تشتمل على ثلاثة علوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for putting the request for help after worship, though help precedes worship in sense, is that the order suits the sūrah’s verse endings.
rows.anchor: ومنه تأخير الاستعانة عن العبادة فى قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the singular “river” stands for plural rivers to match the verse ending; he also allows “river” to mean brightness and spaciousness.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء الأصل الأنهار وإنما وحد لأنه رأس آية

rows.speaker: ابن سيده
rows.claim: Ibn Sīda explains the singular “support” as plural supports, chosen to match the verse endings; “support” means helper.
rows.anchor: قال ابن سيده فى المحكم أى أعضادا وإنما أفرد ليعدل رءوس الآى بالإفراد والعضد المعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “intimate friendships” stands where a singular is intended, as another verse clarifies, to match the verse endings.
rows.anchor: فإن المراد ولا خلة بدليل الآية الأخرى لكن جمعه لأجل مناسبة رءوس الآى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says Arabic can dualize a single place by reference to its two sides; the two gardens may likewise evoke two aspects or directions of the place.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء هذا باب مذهب العرب فى تثنية البقعة الواحدة وجمعها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ also attributes the dual “two gardens” to the rhyme, saying verse endings tolerate additions and omissions that ordinary prose cannot.
rows.anchor: قال وإنما ثناهما لأجل الفاصلة رعاية للتى قبلها والتى بعدها على هذا الوزن

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba rejects changing the promised two gardens into one for rhyme: their dual description, including “both with branches” and “in both,” confirms two.
rows.anchor: وأنكر ذلك ابن قتيبة عليه وأغلظ وقال إنما يجوز فى رءوس الآى زيادة هاء السكت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author suggests the singular “Paradise” in 79:41 may have driven al-Farrāʾ’s rhyme explanation, but the dual “both with branches” remains an objection to it.
rows.anchor: قلت وكأن الملجىء للفراء إلى ذلك قوله تعالى ﴿ وأما من خاف مقام ربه ونهى النفس عن الهوى فإن الجنة هي المأوى ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the familiar labels for stop quality are not a complete, sound classification and have produced confusion in books on pauses.
rows.anchor: فالوجه أن يقال الوقف ضربان اضطرارى واختيارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A forced pause is caused only by running out of breath and is not restricted to particular places; examples include Ḥamza pausing within words or before a genitive complement.
rows.anchor: فالاضطرارى ما يدعو إليه انقطاع النفس فقط وذلك لا يخص موضعا دون موضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An optional pause is preferable and is classified by how the two parts of the statement depend on each other.
rows.anchor: والاختيارى وهو أفضلهما هو الذى لا يكون باعتبار انفصال ما بين جزأى القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A complete pause leaves both adjoining parts independently sufficient; stopping at “we ask for help” is complete because the following request also stands alone.
rows.anchor: الأول التام وهو الذى يكون بحيث يستغنى كل واحد من جزأى القولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An incomplete pause leaves the preceding part sufficient but the following part dependent; one may stop at “straight,” but cannot begin with “the path of those.”
rows.anchor: الثانى الناقص وهو أن يكون ما قبله مستغنيا عما بعده ولا يكون ما بعده مستغنيا عما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author raises the possible objection that an omitted verb could be supplied to govern “the path,” leaving the answer beyond this excerpt.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل ولم لا يجوز أن يقدر هاهنا الفعل الذى ينتصب به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These insights benefit only someone sincere, reflective, and shaped by the Qurʾān in heart and action; otherwise conduct contradicts professed words.
rows.anchor: هذا النوع والذى قبله لن ينتفع به إلا من أخلص لله قلبه ونيته وتدبر الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A spiritual adept feared that relying on another person after praying “You alone we ask for help” would make his prayer a lie; likewise, following Satan’s counsel contradicts seeking refuge from him.
rows.anchor: كما روى أن عارفا وقعت له واقعة فقال له صديق له نستعين بفلان فقال أخشى أن تبطل صلاتى

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh says “woe” here is not a literal prayer, which would sound ugly; it means these people deserve the expression used for ruin and destruction.
rows.anchor: قلت وذكر سيبويه ايضا قوله تعالى ﴿ ويل يومئذ للمكذبين ﴾ 4 ﴿ ويل للمطففين ﴾ 5 فقال لا ينبغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although phrased as statements, “the divorced women wait” and “mothers nurse” are commands, since context shows that treating them as factual reports would entail a falsehood.
rows.anchor: ومنها الامر كقوله تعالى ﴿ والمطلقات يتربصن ﴾ 10 ﴿ والوالدات يرضعن ﴾ 11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prohibition is another speech form illustrated by “None touch it except the purified.”
rows.anchor: ومنها النهي كقوله تعالى ﴿ لا يمسه إلا المطهرون ﴾ 1

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We shall show them Our signs” is given as an example of a promise.
rows.anchor: ومنها الوعد كقوله ﴿ سنريهم آياتنا في الآفاق ﴾ 2

words: وسيَعلم الذين ظلموا أي منقلب ينقلبون
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The wrongdoers will know what fate they will meet” exemplifies a warning.
rows.anchor: ومنها الوعيد كقوله تعالى ﴿ وسيعلم الذين ظلموا أي منقلب ينقلبون ﴾ 3

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Taste! You are the mighty, noble one” is an example of denial and rebuke.
rows.anchor: ومنها الانكار والتبكيت نحو ﴿ ذق إنك أنت العزيز الكريم ﴾ 4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The supplicatory meaning of “we ask for help” is “help us in Your worship.”
rows.anchor: ومنها الدعاء كقوله تعالى ﴿ إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين ﴾ 5 أي أعنا على عبادتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A statement can carry a conditional and its consequence: “We will remove the punishment briefly; you will return” means that if it is removed, they will return.
rows.anchor: وربما كان اللفظ خبرا والمعنى شرطا وجزاء كقوله ﴿ إنا كاشفو العذاب قليلا إنكم عائدون ﴾ 6

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Divorce is twice” means that whoever divorces his wife twice must then either retain her honorably or release her graciously.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله ﴿ الطلاق مرتان ﴾ 8 من طلق امرأته مرتين فليمسكها بعدهما بمعروف أو يسرحها بإحسان

words: فهل لنا من شفعاء فيشفعوا لنا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative “will we have any intercessors?” conveys a wish because the speakers have no real expectation that an intercessor exists there.
rows.anchor: احدها هل كقوله ﴿ فهل لنا من شفعاء فيشفعوا لنا ﴾ 9 حملت هل على إفادة التمني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle “if” can convey a wish with “they wished,” as in 68:9, or without it, as in the other “if only” examples.
rows.anchor: والثاني لو سواء كانت مع ود كقوله تعالى ﴿ ودوا لو تدهن فيدهنون ﴾ 1 بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating a phrase or its equivalent can preserve its meaning from being forgotten when a long interval has passed.
rows.anchor: وحقيقته إعادة اللفظ أو مرادفه لتقرير معنى خشية تناسي الاول لطول العهد به

words: قل الله أعبد مخلصا له ديني
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the cited sūrah, the second “Say, I worship Allah sincerely” serves a new purpose: exclusive worship, marked by fronting the object; the first reports a command to worship.
rows.anchor: لا لتقرير الأول بل لغرض آخر لأن معنى الأول الأمر بالإخبار أنه مأمور بالعبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for repeating “You alone” is emphasis, like repeating “between” in “between Zayd and between ʿAmr.”
rows.anchor: فقيل إنما كررت للتأكيد كما تقول بين زبد وبين عمرو مال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that omission would attach a following pronoun to the second verb and lose the intended emphasis created by placing its object first.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنما كررت لارتفاع أن يتوهم إذا حذفت أن مفعول نستعين ضمير متصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says no explanation for the repeated object is needed: two different verbs each require an object, so stating both is normal and deletion would be exceptional.
rows.anchor: والتحقيق أن السؤال غير متجه لأن هنا عاملين متغايرين كل منهما يقتضي معمولا

words: كَلَّا سَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ ثُمَّ كَلَّا سَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ
rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats the second warning as a new, stronger one rather than mere emphasis; “then” signals its greater force.
rows.anchor: فلهذا قال الزمخشري في قوله تعالى ﴿ كلا سوف تعلمون ثم كلا سوف تعلمون ﴾ 2 إن الثانية تأسيس لا تأكيد

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh says that when coordinated matters are both important, Arabic speakers put first the one that matters more or deserves greater attention; the conjunction itself does not order them.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه كأنهم يقدمون الذي شأنه أهم لهم وهم ببيانه أعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship precedes the request for help because worship is the more important matter.
rows.anchor: وقال تعالى ﴿ إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين ﴾ 5 فقدم العبادة للاهتمام بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two explanations are offered for placing the verb before “in the name of your Lord”: the act is foremost because this was the first revealed sūrah, or the phrase attaches to the second “recite.”
rows.anchor: وأجيب بوجهين أحدهما أن تقديم الفعل هناك أهم لأنها أول سورة نزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting “for Allah” makes the focus of denunciation the attribution of partners to God, rather than the act of making in general.
rows.anchor: لأن الإنكار متوجه إلى الجعل لله لا إلى مطلق الجعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting “partners” before “the jinn,” whose ordinary order would be reversed, makes the reproach and astonishment more forceful.
rows.anchor: والأصل الجن شركاء وقدم لأن المقصود التوبيخ وتقديم الشركاء أبلغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrival of a man from the far end of the city is cited as another example in this discussion of emphatic ordering.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله تعالى في سورة يس ﴿ وجاء من أقصى المدينة رجل يسعى ﴾ 2 وسنذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting the object in “You alone we worship” expresses exclusive worship: we worship You and no one else.
rows.anchor: السابع الاختصاص وذلك بتقديم المفعول والخبر والظرف والجار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fronted object in “if you worship Him” likewise means worshipping Him exclusively.
rows.anchor: وقوله ﴿ إن كنتم إياه تعبدون ﴾ 4 أي إن كنتم تخصونه بالعبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting a predicate is also included among devices for assigning focus; the author cites Abraham’s father’s question and the claim about the people’s fortresses.
rows.anchor: والخبر كقوله ﴿ قال أراغب أنت عن آلهتي ﴾ 5 وقوله ﴿ وظنوا أنهم مانعتهم حصونهم من الله ﴾ 6

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordering “the Knowing” before “the Wise” can show that sound judgment follows knowledge; knowledge may also be first because it is an essential attribute.
rows.anchor: وتقديم العليم على الحكيم لأن الإتقان ناشىء عن العلم

words: لَا عِلْمَ لَنَآ إِلَّا مَا عَلَّمْتَنَآ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this instance, “the Knowing” may be placed first simply to correspond to the preceding “we have no knowledge.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون قدم وصف العلم هنا ليتصل بما يناسبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship comes before seeking aid because it is the cause of receiving aid.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله ﴿ إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين ﴾ 2 قدمت العبادة لأنها سبب حصول الإعانة

words: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلتَّوَّٰبِينَ وَيُحِبُّ ٱلْمُتَطَهِّرِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance is listed before purification because repentance causes purification.
rows.anchor: فإن التوبة سبب الطهارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ordering of “liar” before “sinner” reflects that lying produces sin; the same causal sequence appears in another verse.
rows.anchor: وكذا ﴿ ويل لكل أفاك أثيم ﴾ 4 لأن الإفك سبب الإثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reviving dead land comes first because it enables animal and human life; animals are then mentioned before people because their meat and milk sustain people.
rows.anchor: قدم إحياء الأرض لأنه سبب إحياء الأنعام والأناسي وقدم إحياء الأنعام لأنه مما يحيا به الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth may precede children because it funds marriage and reproduction and enables benefits from children, while its absence can cause hardship for them.
rows.anchor: قيل قدم الأموال من باب تقديم السبب فإنه إنما شرع النكاح عند قدرته على مؤونته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The desires are ranked by natural attachment: women before sons, sons before wealth, gold before silver, and silver before livestock, which is a means to acquiring blessings.
rows.anchor: فلما صدرت الآية بذكر الحب وكان المحبوب مختلف المراتب اقتضت حكمة الترتيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night-journey verse shifts four times between speaking of God in the third person, first-person plural, and third person again; the “show him” form is Hasan’s reading.
rows.anchor: وقد تكرر الالتفات في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fātiḥa begins in third-person style through “Master of the Day of Judgment,” then turns to direct address with “You alone we worship.”
rows.anchor: فإن من أولها إلى قوله ﴿ مالك يوم الدين ﴾ 2 أسلوب غيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah then shifts from direct address in “You bestowed favor” back to third-person wording, saying “not those who incurred anger” rather than “those with whom You were angry.”
rows.anchor: ثم التفت إلى الغيبة بقوله ﴿ غير المغضوب عليهم ﴾ 2 ولم يقل الذين غضبت

rows.speaker: التنوخي والخفاجي وابن الأثير
rows.claim: Al-Tanūkhī, al-Khafājī, Ibn al-Athīr, and others classify the passive “those who incurred anger” after direct address as a shift of style.
rows.anchor: ذكره التنوخي في الأقصى القريب والخفاجي وابن الأثير وغيرهم

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkākī’s account places all six kinds in the final category of iltifāt, the shift by implication.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه على رأى السكاكي تجيء الأقسام الستة في القسم الاخير وهو الانتقال التقديري

words: وَمَا لِيَ لَآ أَعْبُدُ ٱلَّذِى فَطَرَنِى
rows.speaker: صاحب ضوء المصباح
rows.claim: The author of Ḍawʾ al-Miṣbāḥ says only three shifts are used, including substituting address or third-person form for first person, and illustrates one with the believer’s speech.
rows.anchor: وزعم صحاب ضوء المصباح أنه لم يستعمل منها إلا وضع الخطاب والغيبة موضع التكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars count the accusative forms “the patient” and “those who establish prayer” after nominative lists as examples of iltifāt.
rows.anchor: وجعل بعضهم من الالتفات قوله تعالى ﴿ والموفون بعهدهم ﴾ 3 ثم قال ﴿ والصابرين في البأساء والضراء ﴾ 3

rows.speaker: البيانيون
rows.claim: Rhetoricians say changing a style after a long stretch refreshes the listener, draws attention, broadens expression, and eases meter and rhyme.
rows.anchor: وقال البيانيون إن الكلام إذا جاء على أسلوب واحد وطال حسن تغيير الطريقة

rows.speaker: القاضي شمس الدين بن الجوزي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jawzī argues that stylistic variation alone does not explain appropriateness, since a long Qurʾānic list in 33:35 maintains one style throughout.
rows.anchor: ونازعهم القاضي شمس الدين بن الجوزي وقال الظاهر أن مجرد هذا لا يكفي في المناسبة

rows.speaker: القاضي شمس الدين بن الجوزي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jawzī explains the shift from praise to direct address by the listener’s changing attention: the praise awakens the heart, making “You alone” apt.
rows.anchor: فإنه يكون غائبا فيحضر بكلمة واحدة وآخر يكون حاضرا فيغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particular reasons for a shift of style depend on its setting and on the speaker’s purpose.
rows.anchor: وأما الخاصة فتختلف 4 باختلاف محاله ومواقع الكلام فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human beings begin distant from God behind the veil of majesty; knowing and praising Him and worshipping as befits them makes them ready to address Him directly.
rows.anchor: فإذا عرفوه بما هو له وتوسلوا للقرب بالثناء عليه وأقروا بالمحامد له وتعبدوا له بما يليق بهم تأهلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before prayer and intimate address, worshippers should present God’s attributes with reverence, rather than pray carelessly, playfully, or without intention.
rows.anchor: وفيه أنهم يبدون بين يدي كل دعاء له سبحانه ومناجاة له صفات عظمته لمخاطبته على الأدب والتعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intimate prayer rises only after purification from ignorance of God, analogously to bodily prayer after ritual purification; this explains placing refuge-seeking before recitation.
rows.anchor: ومنه أن مناجاته لا تصعد إلا إذا تطهر من أدناس الجهالة به كما لا تسجد الأعضاء إلا بعد التطهير

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the verse’s third-person “the Messenger asks forgiveness for them,” instead of direct “you ask,” magnifies the Messenger’s intercession.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري وكما في قوله تعالى ﴿ ولو أنهم إذ ظلموا أنفسهم جاؤوك فاستغفروا الله واستغفر لهم الرسول ﴾

words: وَمَا لِيَ لَآ أَعْبُدُ ٱلَّذِى فَطَرَنِى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer in Yā-Sīn uses first-person self-advice to soften his counsel to his people; after making his point, “to Him you will return” restores the original address.
rows.anchor: أصل الكلام وما لكم لا تعبدون الذي فطركم ولكنه أبرز الكلام في معرض المناصحة لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the mission “mercy from your Lord” rather than “from Us” completes the point: lordship entails mercy, singles out the Prophet, or marks the Book as sent to him; the text then resumes the pronoun.
rows.anchor: أصل الكلام إنا مرسلين رحمة منا ولكنه وضع الظاهر موضع المضمر للإنذار بأن الربوبية تقتضي الرحمة

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna says that God’s threat to turn the arrogant away from His signs means depriving them of understanding the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان بن عيينة في قوله تعالى : ^ ( سأصرف عن آياتي الذين يتكبرون في الأرض بغير الحق ) ^ ، قال : أحرمهم فهم القرآن

rows.speaker: سفيان الثوري
rows.claim: Sufyān al-Thawrī says understanding the Qurʾān and preoccupation with worldly possessions never coexist in a believer’s heart.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان الثوري : لا يجتمع فهم القرآن والاشتغال بالحطام في قلب مؤمن أبدا

rows.speaker: عبد العزيز بن يحيى الكناني
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Kinānī compares Qurʾānic knowledge to a lion, whose lair only its master can enter.
rows.anchor: قال عبد العزيز بن يحيى الكناني : مثل علم القرآن مثل الأسد لا يمكن من غيله سواه

rows.speaker: ذو النون المصري
rows.claim: Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī says God denies idle hearts access to the Qurʾān’s hidden wisdom.
rows.anchor: قال ذو النون المصري : أبى الله عز وجل [ إلا ] أن يحرم قلوب البطالين مكنون حكمة القرآن

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd interprets “guide us to the straight path” as the Qurʾān, meaning “guide us to its knowledge.”
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن مسعود في قوله تعالى : ^ ( اهدنا الصراط المستقيم ) ^ قال : القرآن ، يقول : أرشدنا إلى علمه

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī says that Qurʾānic knowledge is a reminder known only to discerning men.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن البصري : علم القرآن ذكر لا يعلمه إلا الذكور من الرجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says every discipline is drawn from the Qurʾān and otherwise lacks proof; Ibn Masʿūd’s instruction to “dig into” it refers to foundations of knowledge.
rows.anchor: وكل علم من العلوم منتزع من القرآن

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says anyone seeking knowledge should probe the Qurʾān, since it contains the knowledge of earlier and later peoples; al-Bayhaqī glosses this as the foundations of knowledge.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود : من أراد العلم فليثور القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Companions had distinct specialties: ʿAlī in judging, Zayd in inheritance, Muʿādh in lawful and unlawful matters, and Ubayy in recitation.
rows.anchor: كل منهم مخصوص بنوع من العلم كعلي رضي الله تعالى عنه بالقضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās alone was called an ocean because of his distinctive expertise in exegesis; ʿAlī praised his insight, and Ibn Masʿūd called him an excellent interpreter.
rows.anchor: فلم يسم أحد منهم بحرا إلا عبد الله بن عباس لاختصاصه دونهم بالتفسير وعلم التأويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd died in 32 AH, while Ibn ʿAbbās lived another thirty-six years, prompting the author to reflect on the knowledge he gained afterward.
rows.anchor: وقد مات ابن مسعود في سنة ثنتين وثلاثين

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī had prior expertise in interpreting the Fātiḥa and said he could dictate a camel-load of commentary on it.
rows.anchor: وهو القائل : لو أردت أن أملي وقر بعير على الفاتحة لفعلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors the view that sūrah order is established by revelation and says each sūrah’s opening closely or subtly fits the ending of the preceding one.
rows.anchor: قلت وهو مبنى على أن ترتيب السور توقيفى وهذا الراجح كما سيأتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anʿām’s opening praise fits al-Māʾida’s ending, where judgment is completed and praise is voiced.
rows.anchor: كافتتاح سورة الأنعام بالحمد فإنه مناسب لختام سورة المائدة من فصل القضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fāṭir’s opening praise connects to the preceding sūrah’s description of a barrier between people and what they desire, as well as the destruction of wrongdoers ending in praise.
rows.anchor: وكافتتاح سورة فاطر ب ﴿ الحمد ﴾ أيضا فإنه مناسب لختام ما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥadīd opens with glorification, matching the preceding al-Wāqiʿa’s command to glorify God.
rows.anchor: وكافتتاح سورة الحديد بالتسبيح فإنه مناسب لختام سورة الواقعة من الأمر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara’s opening, “This is the Book, without doubt,” answers al-Fātiḥa’s request for guidance: this Book is the straight path requested, resolving al-Zamakhsharī’s question about the connection.
rows.anchor: كأنهم لما سألوا الهداية إلى الصراط المستقيم قيل لهم ذلك الصراط الذى سألتم

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says the connection of Quraysh to al-Fīl resembles the narrative in which Pharaoh’s household takes up Moses, who becomes their enemy and grief.
rows.anchor: حتى قال الأخفش اتصالها بها من باب قوله ﴿ فالتقطه آل فرعون ليكون لهم عدوا وحزنا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kawthar counters al-Māʿūn: abundant divine giving answers the previous sūrah’s stinginess.
rows.anchor: فذكر هنا فى مقابلة البخل ﴿ إنا أعطيناك الكوثر ﴾ أى الكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kawthar’s command to pray answers al-Māʿūn’s criticism of abandoning prayer, while praying “to your Lord” answers ostentation by directing worship to God’s approval.
rows.anchor: وفى مقابلة ترك الصلاة فصل أى دم عليها وفى مقابلة الرياء ﴿ لربك ﴾ أى لرضاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to sacrifice answers al-Māʿūn’s charge of withholding help: the sacrificial meat is to be given in charity.
rows.anchor: وفى مقابلة منع الماعون ﴿ وانحر ﴾ وأراد به التصدق بلحم الأضاحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Isrāʾ opens with glorification and al-Kahf with praise, reflecting the usual order of the paired phrases “Glory be to God, and praise be to God.”
rows.anchor: وكذلك مناسبة فاتحة سورة الإسراء بالتسبيح وسورة الكهف بالتحميد لأن التسبيح حيث جاء مقدم على التحميد
